questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An athlete runs along a semicircular track of radius $R = 14\text{ m}$ from point $A$ to point $B$ across the diameter. What are the total distance traveled and the magnitude of the athlete's displacement vector? (Take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Single point-mass athlete
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with origin at center O of semicircle

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Distinguishing the scalar curved arc path integral pi*R from the vector end-to-end diameter 2R.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires geometric evaluation of circumference arc vs diameter, not bare recall.

A.diagnostic: Correctly computed distance = pi * R = 44 m and displacement magnitude = 2R = 28 m.

B.diagnostic: Equated displacement magnitude with distance traveled, ignoring straight-line shortcut.

C.diagnostic: Swapped the definitions of distance and displacement.

D.diagnostic: Used the full circle perimeter 2*pi*R = 88 m instead of the semicircle arc.

progressive_hints.title: Definitions of Distance vs Displacement
progressive_hints.text: Distance is the actual length of the path traversed. Displacement is the straight-line directed distance from initial to final position.

progressive_hints.title: Arc and Diameter Formulae
progressive_hints.text: The path is a semicircle: $\text{Distance} = \pi R$. The end points $A$ and $B$ lie across the diameter: $|\Delta\vec{r}| = 2R$.

progressive_hints.title: Numerical Computation
progressive_hints.text: Calculate $\pi R = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 44\text{ m}$ and $2R = 2 \times 14 = 28\text{ m}$.

derivation_steps: Athlete travels along the circumference of a semicircle: $s = \pi R = \frac{22}{7} \times 14\text{ m} = 44\text{ m}$.
Displacement is the vector connecting start point A to end point B: $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A$.
Points A and B are diametrically opposite on the circle, so the straight-line distance is the diameter: $|\Delta\vec{r}| = 2R = 2 \times 14\text{ m} = 28\text{ m}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: Distance -> 0 and Displacement -> 0 (Point particle at rest)
Distance >= Displacement (44 m > 28 m, strictly satisfies inequality)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A car travels the first half of a total distance $d$ at a uniform speed of $30\text{ km/h}$ and the remaining half of the distance at a uniform speed of $60\text{ km/h}$. What is the average speed of the car for the entire journey?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Single automobile moving in a 1D straight line
system_parameters.reference_frame: Ground frame (+x along direction of motion)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling average speed as total distance over total time, arriving at the harmonic mean rather than arithmetic mean.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires algebraic rate modeling across unequal time segments.

A.diagnostic: Correctly applied harmonic mean: v_avg = 2*v1*v2 / (v1 + v2) = 2(30)(60) / 90 = 40 km/h.

B.diagnostic: Fell into the classic arithmetic mean trap: (30 + 60) / 2 = 45 km/h, ignoring time weighting.

C.diagnostic: Calculated (2 * 60 * 30) / (60 + 30) incorrectly or guessed midpoint value.

D.diagnostic: Applied geometric mean sqrt(30 * 60) = sqrt(1800) approx 42.4 km/h or miscomputed harmonic.

progressive_hints.title: Fundamental Definition of Average Speed
progressive_hints.text: Average speed is defined as total distance divided by total time: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{d_{\text{total}}}{t_{\text{total}}}$.

progressive_hints.title: Time for Each Distance Half
progressive_hints.text: Let each half be $s = d/2$. Time for first half is $t_1 = \frac{s}{30}$, time for second half is $t_2 = \frac{s}{60}$.

progressive_hints.title: Summing Time and Dividing
progressive_hints.text: Total time is $t = s(\frac{1}{30} + \frac{1}{60}) = s(\frac{3}{60}) = \frac{s}{20} = \frac{d}{40}$. Hence $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{d}{d/40} = 40\text{ km/h}$.

derivation_steps: Let total distance be $d$. Each half has length $s = d/2$.
Time taken for first half: $t_1 = \frac{d/2}{v_1} = \frac{d}{2(30)} = \frac{d}{60}$.
Time taken for second half: $t_2 = \frac{d/2}{v_2} = \frac{d}{2(60)} = \frac{d}{120}$.
Total elapsed time: $t_{\text{total}} = t_1 + t_2 = \frac{d}{60} + \frac{d}{120} = \frac{3d}{120} = \frac{d}{40}$.
Average speed: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{d}{t_{\text{total}}} = \frac{d}{d/40} = 40\text{ km/h}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: v_avg = 2*v*v / (2v) = v (Uniform velocity recovered)
v_avg -> 0 (Vehicle never completes the first half; average speed drops to zero)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A tennis ball is projected vertically upward into the air. At the exact instant the ball reaches its highest point (apex), what are its instantaneous velocity and instantaneous acceleration? (Take upward as positive and magnitude of gravitational acceleration as $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Isolated tennis ball under gravitational field
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with upward chosen as positive (+y)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Dismantling the intuitive misconception that zero instantaneous velocity entails zero acceleration.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires conceptual explanation of velocity turnaround vs constant downward field acceleration.

A.diagnostic: Correctly identified that velocity momentarily passes through zero while acceleration remains constant -g downward.

B.diagnostic: Fell into the primary apex trap, assuming zero velocity means zero force and zero acceleration.

C.diagnostic: Assigned the numerical value of gravitational acceleration to velocity.

D.diagnostic: Selected upward (+9.8 m/s^2) for gravity instead of downward (-9.8 m/s^2).

progressive_hints.title: Turnaround Point
progressive_hints.text: At the apex, the ball stops rising and is about to start falling. What is its speed at this exact turnaround instant?

progressive_hints.title: Unbroken Gravitational Interaction
progressive_hints.text: Does Earth's gravity turn off when an object stops moving? Newton's law of gravity acts continuously downward on the mass.

progressive_hints.title: Acceleration as Derivative
progressive_hints.text: Acceleration is $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$. Even though $v = 0$ at one instant, the slope $\frac{dv}{dt} = -g = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ is constant throughout.

derivation_steps: Vertical position is $y(t) = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
Instantaneous velocity is $v(t) = \frac{dy}{dt} = u - gt$.
At the highest point $t = t_{\text{apex}} = \frac{u}{g}$, substituting yields $v(t_{\text{apex}}) = u - g\left(\frac{u}{g}\right) = 0\text{ m/s}$.
Instantaneous acceleration is $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(u - gt) = -g = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.
Acceleration is constant throughout the entire trajectory, including the apex instant.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: dv/dt = 0 => velocity would remain zero forever; ball would float in mid-air indefinitely (refuting option B)
Ball moves with constant upward velocity u without an apex

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A steel ball is released from rest from the top of a tall tower. According to Galileo's law of odd numbers for uniform acceleration from rest, what is the ratio of the distance fallen during the $3^{\text{rd}}$ second to the distance fallen during the $1^{\text{st}}$ second?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Point-mass steel ball in free fall

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying the nth-second displacement formula s_n = u + 0.5*a*(2n - 1) for n=1 and n=3.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires evaluating the discrete interval ratio rather than reciting the law's name.

A.diagnostic: Correctly applied Galileo's odd-number rule: Delta s_n proportional to (2n - 1). For n=3, 2(3)-1 = 5, giving ratio 5 : 1.

B.diagnostic: Assumed linear index ratio 3 : 1 instead of odd-number ratio.

C.diagnostic: Confused displacement in the 3rd second with total cumulative displacement after 3 seconds: s(3) / s(1) = 3^2 / 1^2 = 9 : 1.

D.diagnostic: Subtracted indices incorrectly or assumed even-number pattern.

progressive_hints.title: Displacement in the nth Second
progressive_hints.text: The formula for distance covered in the $n^{\text{th}}$ second when starting from rest ($u=0$) is $s_n = \frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1)$.

progressive_hints.title: Form the Ratio
progressive_hints.text: Divide $s_3$ by $s_1$: $\frac{s_3}{s_1} = \frac{5}{1}$, yielding the ratio $5 : 1$.

derivation_steps: Distance covered in $t$ seconds from rest is $s(t) = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
Distance in 1st second: $s_1 = s(1) - s(0) = \frac{1}{2}g(1^2 - 0^2) = \frac{1}{2}g(1)$.
The ratio is $\frac{s_3}{s_1} = \frac{5}{1} = 5 : 1$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: Successive second distances ratio: 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 : 9 (strictly confirms 5 for 3rd second)
Distance fallen in 1st second is s1 = 0.5 * g * (1)^2 = 0.5 g

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: The velocity-time graph of a particle moving along a straight line is shown in Figure KIN-02. The particle starts at $v = +10\text{ m/s}$ at $t = 0\text{ s}$, decelerates uniformly to $0\text{ m/s}$ at $t = 2\text{ s}$, and continues accelerating uniformly in the negative direction to $-10\text{ m/s}$ at $t = 4\text{ s}$. What are the net displacement and the total distance traveled by the particle over the interval from $t = 0$ to $t = 4\text{ s}$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Single point particle in 1D rectilinear motion
system_parameters.reference_frame: 1D Cartesian frame (+x along initial velocity direction)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Interpreting signed area under v-t graph for vector displacement versus absolute sum of areas for scalar distance.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dual representation translation from graph geometry to physical quantities.

A.diagnostic: Correctly integrated signed area (+10 - 10 = 0 m for displacement) and absolute area (10 + 10 = 20 m for distance).

B.diagnostic: Treated the area below the time axis as positive for displacement, conflating distance with displacement.

C.diagnostic: Calculated only the first triangle area (0.5 * 2 * 10 = 10 m) and neglected the second half.

D.diagnostic: Subtracted areas with an erroneous negative net residual.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Meaning of Area under v-t Graph
progressive_hints.text: The area between the velocity-time graph and the time axis represents displacement. Area above the axis is positive; area below is negative.

progressive_hints.title: Computing Triangle Areas
progressive_hints.text: First triangle ($0$ to $2\text{ s}$): $\text{Area}_1 = \frac{1}{2}(2)(10) = +10\text{ m}$. Second triangle ($2$ to $4\text{ s}$): $\text{Area}_2 = \frac{1}{2}(2)(-10) = -10\text{ m}$.

progressive_hints.title: Displacement vs Distance Integration
progressive_hints.text: Displacement $= \text{Area}_1 + \text{Area}_2 = +10 - 10 = 0\text{ m}$. Distance $= |\text{Area}_1| + |\text{Area}_2| = 10 + 10 = 20\text{ m}$.

derivation_steps: Displacement is given by the definite integral: $\Delta x = \int_0^4 v(t)\,dt$.
From $t=0$ to $t=2\text{ s}$: $\text{Area}_1 = \frac{1}{2} \times 2\text{ s} \times 10\text{ m/s} = +10\text{ m}$.
From $t=2$ to $t=4\text{ s}$: $\text{Area}_2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 2\text{ s} \times (-10\text{ m/s}) = -10\text{ m}$.
Net displacement: $\Delta x = (+10\text{ m}) + (-10\text{ m}) = 0\text{ m}$.
Total distance traveled is the integral of speed: $s = \int_0^4 |v(t)|\,dt = |+10\text{ m}| + |-10\text{ m}| = 20\text{ m}$.

limiting_cases.condition: Particle returns to initial coordinate x(0)
limiting_cases.expected_outcome: Displacement identically zero (0 m), Distance strictly positive (20 m)
Velocity remains constant; displacement is purely v * t

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A marksman fires a rifle horizontally at $u = 200\text{ m/s}$ from the edge of a vertical cliff of height $H = 45\text{ m}$ above a level plain. Simultaneously, a bullet casing is dropped from rest from the same height. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$ and neglecting air resistance, what is the time taken by the fired bullet to reach the ground, and what is its horizontal impact distance from the base of the cliff?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Fired projectile bullet and dropped casing
system_parameters.reference_frame: 2D Cartesian frame with origin at cliff base (+x forward, +y upward)
idealizations: Horizontal launch initial vertical velocity u_y = 0

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling vertical free fall independently from horizontal uniform motion, refuting the belief that horizontal speed alters drop time.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires 2D component decoupling and algebraic evaluation.

A.diagnostic: Correctly solved t = sqrt(2H/g) = sqrt(90/10) = 3 s and x = u_x * t = 200 * 3 = 600 m.

B.diagnostic: Assumed the high horizontal speed keeps the bullet airborne longer (t = 4.5 s).

C.diagnostic: Calculated time correctly (3 s) but forgot to multiply speed by time: used x = 200 m.

D.diagnostic: Used t = sqrt(H/g) = sqrt(4.5) approx 2 s instead of sqrt(2H/g).

progressive_hints.title: Galilean Orthogonal Independence
progressive_hints.text: The vertical motion is completely independent of the horizontal velocity. The initial vertical velocity is $u_y = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Vertical Fall Time Equation
progressive_hints.text: Apply $H = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 \implies t = \sqrt{\frac{2H}{g}}$. Both the fired bullet and the dropped casing hit the ground at the same instant.

progressive_hints.title: Horizontal Range
progressive_hints.text: Calculate $t = \sqrt{\frac{2(45)}{10}} = \sqrt{9} = 3\text{ s}$. Horizontal distance is $x = u_x \times t = 200 \times 3 = 600\text{ m}$.

derivation_steps: Vertical motion is governed by $y(t) = H - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
At ground contact $y(t) = 0 \implies t = \sqrt{\frac{2H}{g}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 45\text{ m}}{10\text{ m/s}^2}} = \sqrt{9\text{ s}^2} = 3\text{ s}$.
Horizontal motion has zero acceleration ($a_x = 0$): $x(t) = u_x t$.
Impact range: $x = 200\text{ m/s} \times 3\text{ s} = 600\text{ m}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: x -> 0 while drop time remains t = 3 s (Pure 1D drop recovered)
t -> 0 and x -> 0 (Instant ground contact)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upward from the ground with an initial speed $u = 40\text{ m/s}$. At what two distinct times $t_1$ and $t_2$ during its flight does the ball pass an observation platform located at a height $h = 60\text{ m}$ above the ground? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Single point projectile under 1D gravity

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Setting up and solving the quadratic equation 0.5*g*t^2 - u*t + h = 0 and verifying root sum/product invariants.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires solving quadratic equation and kinematic time-reversal decomposition.

A.diagnostic: Correctly factored t^2 - 8t + 12 = (t - 2)(t - 6) = 0, giving t1 = 2 s (ascent) and t2 = 6 s (descent).

B.diagnostic: Selected roots with sum 8 but product 15 != 12.

C.diagnostic: Selected roots with sum 8 but product 7 != 12.

D.diagnostic: Included the apex time t = 4 s instead of the second passage time.

progressive_hints.title: Equation of Motion for Vertical Throw
progressive_hints.text: Set up the displacement equation: $h = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ with $u = 40\text{ m/s}, g = 10\text{ m/s}^2, h = 60\text{ m}$.

progressive_hints.title: Standard Quadratic Form
progressive_hints.text: Substitute the numbers: $60 = 40t - 5t^2 \implies 5t^2 - 40t + 60 = 0$. Divide through by 5 to obtain $t^2 - 8t + 12 = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Factoring the Quadratic
progressive_hints.text: Factor $(t - 2)(t - 6) = 0$. The roots are $t_1 = 2\text{ s}$ on the way up and $t_2 = 6\text{ s}$ on the way down.

derivation_steps: Position as a function of time: $y(t) = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = 40t - 5t^2$.
Factoring yields $(t - 2)(t - 6) = 0 \implies t_1 = 2\text{ s}, \quad t_2 = 6\text{ s}$.
Check via sum of roots: $t_1 + t_2 = 8\text{ s} = \frac{2u}{g} = T$ (total flight time).
Check via product of roots: $t_1 t_2 = 2 \times 6 = 12\text{ s}^2 = \frac{2h}{g} = \frac{2(60)}{10} = 12\text{ s}^2$.

limiting_cases.condition: Apex passage h = H_max = u^2/(2g) = 80 m
limiting_cases.expected_outcome: t1 = t2 = 4 s (Roots coalesce at apex turnaround)
t1 = 0 s and t2 = 8 s (Launch and landing)

questions.stem: An ideal projectile is launched from ground level with speed $u = 20\sqrt{2}\text{ m/s}$ at an elevation angle of $\theta = 45^\circ$ above the horizontal (Figure KIN-03). Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what are the coordinates $(x_{\text{apex}}, y_{\text{apex}})$ of the trajectory's highest point and the total horizontal range $R$ upon landing?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Point projectile under 2D planar gravity
system_parameters.reference_frame: 2D Cartesian ground frame with launch at (0, 0)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Resolving initial vector u into equal components ux=uy=20 m/s and computing parabolic landmarks (R/2, H) and range R.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires geometric vector decomposition and landmark coordinate synthesis.

A.diagnostic: Correctly computed u_x = u_y = 20 m/s, H = 20^2 / (2*10) = 20 m, x_apex = 20*2 = 40 m, and R = 2 * x_apex = 80 m.

B.diagnostic: Swapped the horizontal and vertical apex coordinates.

C.diagnostic: Used H = u_y^2 / g = 40 m instead of u_y^2 / (2g).

D.diagnostic: Doubled the horizontal coordinates mistakenly.

progressive_hints.title: Resolve Initial Velocity
progressive_hints.text: At $\theta = 45^\circ$, $u_x = u\cos 45^\circ = 20\sqrt{2} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 20\text{ m/s}$ and $u_y = 20\text{ m/s}$.

progressive_hints.title: Time to Apex and Maximum Height
progressive_hints.text: Time to apex is $t_{\text{apex}} = \frac{u_y}{g} = \frac{20}{10} = 2\text{ s}$. Maximum height is $H = \frac{u_y^2}{2g} = \frac{400}{20} = 20\text{ m}$.

progressive_hints.title: Horizontal Coordinates
progressive_hints.text: Horizontal position at apex is $x_{\text{apex}} = u_x \times t_{\text{apex}} = 20 \times 2 = 40\text{ m}$. By symmetry, range is $R = 2 \times 40 = 80\text{ m}$.

derivation_steps: Decompose launch velocity: $u_x = 20\sqrt{2}\cos 45^\circ = 20\text{ m/s}$, $u_y = 20\sqrt{2}\sin 45^\circ = 20\text{ m/s}$.
Apex occurs when vertical velocity is zero: $v_y(t) = u_y - gt = 0 \implies t_{\text{apex}} = \frac{20}{10} = 2\text{ s}$.
Maximum height coordinate: $y_{\text{apex}} = H = u_y t_{\text{apex}} - \frac{1}{2}g t_{\text{apex}}^2 = 20(2) - 5(4) = 20\text{ m}$.
Horizontal apex coordinate: $x_{\text{apex}} = u_x t_{\text{apex}} = 20 \times 2 = 40\text{ m}$.
Total flight time $T = 2 t_{\text{apex}} = 4\text{ s}$. Horizontal range $R = u_x T = 20 \times 4 = 80\text{ m}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: x_apex = R / 2 (40 m = 80 m / 2, strictly symmetric)

questions.stem: Two projectiles are launched from the same ground origin with identical initial speed $u$, one at angle $\theta_1 = 30^\circ$ and the other at angle $\theta_2 = 60^\circ$ to the horizontal. Let $R_1, R_2$ be their horizontal ranges, and $T_1, T_2$ be their total times of flight. Which statement correctly describes their ranges and the product of their flight times $T_1 T_2$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two independent projectiles launched under uniform gravity

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Proving range degeneracy for complementary angles sin(2*theta) = sin(2*(90-theta)) and evaluating flight time product.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires algebraic proof linking product of flight times to common range.

A.diagnostic: Correctly proved that complementary angles produce identical range R and T1*T2 = (2u sin 30 / g)(2u sin 60 / g) = 2R/g.

B.diagnostic: Believed higher launch angle always produces greater horizontal range.

C.diagnostic: Misplaced a factor of 4 in the product of flight times.

D.diagnostic: Assumed lower launch angle gives longer range and multiplied factor of 2 incorrectly.

progressive_hints.title: Range Formula for Complementary Angles
progressive_hints.text: Horizontal range is $R = \frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$. Notice that $\sin(2 \times 30^\circ) = \sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, and $\sin(2 \times 60^\circ) = \sin 120^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

progressive_hints.title: Flight Time Product
progressive_hints.text: The flight times are $T_1 = \frac{2u\sin 30^\circ}{g}$ and $T_2 = \frac{2u\sin 60^\circ}{g}$.

progressive_hints.title: Multiply T1 and T2
progressive_hints.text: $T_1 T_2 = \frac{4u^2 \sin 30^\circ \cos 30^\circ}{g^2} = \frac{2}{g} \left(\frac{u^2 \sin 60^\circ}{g}\right) = \frac{2R}{g}$.

derivation_steps: Range formula: $R(\theta) = \frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$.
Since $\sin(2(90^\circ - \theta)) = \sin(180^\circ - 2\theta) = \sin 2\theta$, complementary angles produce identical range: $R_1 = R_2 = R$.
Flight times: $T_1 = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$, $T_2 = \frac{2u\cos\theta}{g}$.
Product: $T_1 T_2 = \frac{4u^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta}{g^2} = \frac{2}{g} \left(\frac{u^2 (2\sin\theta\cos\theta)}{g}\right) = \frac{2}{g} \left(\frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}\right) = \frac{2R}{g}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: T1 = T2 = T_max_range => T^2 = (2u sin 45 / g)^2 = 2u^2 / g^2 = 2R_max / g (Exact match)
Average speed equals instantaneous speed

questions.stem: A car negotiates a horizontal circular roundabout of radius $r = 20\text{ m}$ at a constant speed of $v = 10\text{ m/s}$. What is the magnitude of the car's acceleration, and in what direction does it act?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Automobile modeled as point mass

options.A: Magnitude $= 5\text{ m/s}^2$, directed radially inward toward the center
options.B: Magnitude $= 0\text{ m/s}^2$, because the speed is constant
options.C: Magnitude $= 5\text{ m/s}^2$, directed tangentially along the velocity

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying centripetal acceleration formula a_c = v^2/r and recognizing that changing direction constitutes non-zero inward acceleration.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires evaluating both magnitude and vector direction under UCM constraints.

A.diagnostic: Correctly computed a_c = v^2 / r = 10^2 / 20 = 5 m/s^2 directed radially inward toward the center of curvature.

B.diagnostic: Fell into the constant-speed trap, assuming zero rate of speed change implies zero acceleration vector.

C.diagnostic: Assumed acceleration is tangential in the direction of motion, which would change the speed.

D.diagnostic: Computed v / r = 10 / 20 = 0.5 (angular speed omega) and claimed outward direction.

progressive_hints.title: Vector Velocity in Circular Motion
progressive_hints.text: Even though the speed (magnitude of velocity) is constant, the direction of the velocity vector is continuously changing.

progressive_hints.title: Centripetal Acceleration Formula
progressive_hints.text: A continuous change in direction requires an acceleration perpendicular to velocity, directed toward the center: $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$.

progressive_hints.title: Numerical Evaluation
progressive_hints.text: Substitute $v = 10\text{ m/s}$ and $r = 20\text{ m}$: $a_c = \frac{10^2}{20} = \frac{100}{20} = 5\text{ m/s}^2$, directed radially inward.

derivation_steps: Position vector in uniform circular motion: $\vec{r}(t) = r\cos(\omega t)\hat{i} + r\sin(\omega t)\hat{j}$.
Velocity: $\vec{v}(t) = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = -r\omega\sin(\omega t)\hat{i} + r\omega\cos(\omega t)\hat{j}$. Speed is $|ec{v}| = r\omega = v = \text{constant}$.
Acceleration: $\vec{a}(t) = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = -r\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\hat{i} - r\omega^2\sin(\omega t)\hat{j} = -\omega^2 \vec{r}(t)$.
Direction is strictly opposite to the position vector (pointing radially inward toward center).
Magnitude: $a = \omega^2 r = \left(\frac{v}{r}\right)^2 r = \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{10^2}{20} = 5\text{ m/s}^2$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: a_c -> 0 (Zero acceleration in uniform straight-line motion)
a_c -> 0 (Stationary body)

questions.stem: Raindrops are falling vertically downward at a terminal speed of $12\text{ m/s}$. A cyclist rides horizontally due East at a steady speed of $5\text{ m/s}$. At what angle to the vertical must the cyclist hold an umbrella to best protect themselves from the rain, and what is the relative speed of the raindrops with respect to the cyclist?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Falling raindrops and moving cyclist

options.A: Relative Speed $= 13\text{ m/s}$, tilted at $\arctan(5/12) \approx 22.6^\circ$ toward the East
options.B: Relative Speed $= 17\text{ m/s}$, tilted at $45^\circ$ toward the East
options.C: Relative Speed $= 13\text{ m/s}$, tilted at $\arctan(12/5) \approx 67.4^\circ$ toward the East
options.D: Relative Speed $= 7\text{ m/s}$, held vertically upward ($0^\circ$)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying Galilean relative velocity subtraction v_rel = v_rain - v_cyclist and evaluating the resulting right triangle.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires relative vector model construction and orientation angle determination.

A.diagnostic: Correctly computed v_rel = sqrt(12^2 + 5^2) = 13 m/s and tan(theta) = v_cyclist / v_rain = 5/12.

B.diagnostic: Added speeds scalar-wise (12 + 5 = 17 m/s) ignoring vector orthogonality.

C.diagnostic: Calculated angle relative to the horizontal (tan = 12/5) instead of relative to the vertical.

D.diagnostic: Subtracted speeds algebraically (12 - 5 = 7 m/s) and ignored forward tilt.

progressive_hints.title: Relative Velocity Vector Equation
progressive_hints.text: The velocity of rain relative to the cyclist is $\vec{v}_{\text{rel}} = \vec{v}_{\text{rain}} - \vec{v}_{\text{cyclist}}$.

progressive_hints.title: Vector Components
progressive_hints.text: With $+x$ East and $+y$ Up: $\vec{v}_{\text{rain}} = -12\hat{j}$ and $\vec{v}_{\text{cyclist}} = 5\hat{i}$. Thus $\vec{v}_{\text{rel}} = -5\hat{i} - 12\hat{j}$.

progressive_hints.title: Magnitude and Angle
progressive_hints.text: Magnitude is $|\vec{v}_{\text{rel}}| = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + (-12)^2} = 13\text{ m/s}$. The angle with the vertical is $\tan\theta = \frac{|v_x|}{|v_y|} = \frac{5}{12}$ toward the East.

derivation_steps: Velocity of rain in ground frame: $\vec{v}_r = -12\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$.
Velocity of cyclist in ground frame: $\vec{v}_c = +5\hat{i}\text{ m/s}$.
Relative velocity of rain with respect to cyclist: $\vec{v}_{r/c} = \vec{v}_r - \vec{v}_c = -5\hat{i} - 12\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$.
Relative speed: $|ec{v}_{r/c}| = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + (-12)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13\text{ m/s}$.
To intercept the raindrops, the umbrella must point opposite to $\vec{v}_{r/c}$, i.e., along $+5\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}$.
Angle with the vertical: $\tan\theta = \frac{v_c}{v_r} = \frac{5}{12} \implies \theta = \arctan(5/12) \approx 22.6^\circ$ tilted toward the forward direction (East).

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: v_rel -> 12 m/s, theta -> 0 deg (Umbrella held straight up)
theta -> 90 deg (Horizontal rush of air/mist)

questions.stem: A test vehicle starts from rest ($u = 0$) at $t = 0\text{ s}$ and experiences a triangular acceleration pulse as shown in Figure KIN-04. The acceleration increases linearly from $0$ to a maximum of $4\text{ m/s}^2$ at $t = 3\text{ s}$, then decreases linearly back to $0$ at $t = 6\text{ s}$. What is the final velocity of the vehicle at $t = 6\text{ s}$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Test vehicle moving in a 1D straight line

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating the definite integral of a variable acceleration pulse via triangular geometric area Delta v = 0.5 * base * height.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires calculus-graph area synthesis for non-constant acceleration.

A.diagnostic: Correctly computed Delta v = Area = 0.5 * base * height = 0.5 * 6 * 4 = 12 m/s.

B.diagnostic: Treated the pulse as a rectangle: base * height = 6 * 4 = 24 m/s.

C.diagnostic: Calculated only half of the triangle area: 0.5 * 3 * 4 = 6 m/s.

D.diagnostic: Averaged maximum and minimum incorrectly or added arbitrary offsets.

progressive_hints.title: Fundamental Relation between Acceleration and Velocity
progressive_hints.text: By definition, $a = \frac{dv}{dt} \implies \Delta v = v(t) - v(0) = \int_0^t a(t')\,dt'$.

progressive_hints.title: Area of Acceleration-Time Graph
progressive_hints.text: The integral $\int_0^6 a(t)\,dt$ represents the area under the acceleration-time curve.

progressive_hints.title: Triangular Area Calculation
progressive_hints.text: The graph is a triangle with base $b = 6\text{ s}$ and height $h = 4\text{ m/s}^2$: $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 4 = 12\text{ m/s}$.

derivation_steps: From the definition of acceleration: $dv = a(t)\,dt$.
Integrating from $t = 0$ to $t = 6\text{ s}$: $v(6) - v(0) = \int_0^6 a(t)\,dt$.
The area under the $a$-$t$ curve is a single triangle: $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 6\text{ s} \times 4\text{ m/s}^2 = 12\text{ m/s}$.
Since the vehicle starts from rest ($v(0) = 0$), $v(6) = 12\text{ m/s}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: Delta v -> 0 (Zero acceleration leaves velocity unchanged at 0 m/s)
a_avg = Area / duration = 12 / 6 = 2 m/s^2; v = a_avg * t = 2 * 6 = 12 m/s (Perfect match)

questions.stem: Two projectiles are launched simultaneously from points on level ground separated by a horizontal distance $d = 100\text{ m}$. Particle 1 is launched from $(0, 0)$ with speed $u_1 = 20\text{ m/s}$ at an elevation angle of $30^\circ$. Particle 2 is launched from $(100\text{ m}, 0)$ toward Particle 1 with speed $u_2$ at an elevation angle of $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what must be the speed $u_2$ for the two projectiles to collide in mid-air, and at what time $t$ after launch does the collision occur?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two interacting projectiles in free fall
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame (+x from Particle 1 to Particle 2, +y upward)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Exploiting zero relative acceleration a_rel = 0 to establish equal vertical velocity matching u1y = u2y and solving for collision time.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires relative frame elimination of gravity and dual kinematic constraint coupling.

A.diagnostic: Correctly deduced u_2 = 20 m/s from u1*sin(30) = u2*sin(30), and t = d / (u1x + u2x) = 100 / (40 cos 30) = 5/sqrt(3) s.

B.diagnostic: Doubled u2 arbitrarily and used t = 5 s.

C.diagnostic: Computed u2 correctly but used t = d / u1 = 100 / 20 = 5 s ignoring particle 2's approach velocity.

D.diagnostic: Used horizontal component instead of total speed for u2.

progressive_hints.title: Zero Relative Acceleration
progressive_hints.text: Both particles experience the exact same downward acceleration $\vec{g}$. Therefore, their relative acceleration is $\vec{a}_{1/2} = \vec{g} - \vec{g} = \vec{0}$.

progressive_hints.title: Vertical Alignment Condition
progressive_hints.text: In the relative frame, the motion is a straight line. For a horizontal collision, the relative vertical velocity must be zero: $u_1\sin 30^\circ = u_2\sin 30^\circ \implies u_2 = 20\text{ m/s}$.

progressive_hints.title: Closing Speed and Collision Time
progressive_hints.text: The horizontal closing speed is $v_{\text{close}} = u_1\cos 30^\circ + u_2\cos 30^\circ = 40\cos 30^\circ = 20\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}$. Collision time is $t = \frac{100}{20\sqrt{3}} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ s}$.

derivation_steps: Relative acceleration: $\vec{a}_{1/2} = \vec{a}_1 - \vec{a}_2 = (-g\hat{j}) - (-g\hat{j}) = \vec{0}$.
Relative trajectory is a straight line: $\vec{r}_{1/2}(t) = \vec{r}_{1/2}(0) + \vec{v}_{1/2} t$.
Initial separation is purely horizontal: $\vec{r}_2(0) - \vec{r}_1(0) = 100\hat{i}\text{ m}$.
For collision, relative velocity must point purely along the x-axis: $v_{y, \text{rel}} = u_1\sin 30^\circ - u_2\sin 30^\circ = 0 \implies u_2 = u_1 = 20\text{ m/s}$.
Horizontal relative speed: $v_{x, \text{rel}} = u_1\cos 30^\circ - (-u_2\cos 30^\circ) = 2(20\cos 30^\circ) = 20\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}$.
Collision time: $t = \frac{d}{v_{x, \text{rel}}} = \frac{100\text{ m}}{20\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ s} \approx 2.89\text{ s}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: t -> 0 (Instantaneous coincidence)

questions.stem: An ideal projectile is launched with speed $u$ at an elevation angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. In terms of $u, \theta,$ and $g$, what is the radius of curvature $\rho_{\text{apex}}$ of the parabolic trajectory at its highest point?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Point projectile along parabolic curve

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesizing the differential definition of radius of curvature rho = v^2 / a_perp with apex velocity v = u*cos(theta) and a_perp = g.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires synthesizing differential curvature geometry with projectile kinematics.

A.diagnostic: Correctly evaluated rho = v^2 / a_perp = (u cos theta)^2 / g at the apex.

B.diagnostic: Used vertical component u*sin(theta) instead of horizontal component u*cos(theta).

C.diagnostic: Neglected angle dependence, using full launch speed u instead of apex speed.

D.diagnostic: Omitted the squaring of the cosine factor in v^2.

progressive_hints.title: Definition of Radius of Curvature
progressive_hints.text: For any curved path, the radius of curvature $\rho$ is related to normal acceleration by $a_\perp = \frac{v^2}{\rho} \implies \rho = \frac{v^2}{a_\perp}$.

progressive_hints.title: Apex Kinematic State
progressive_hints.text: At the apex, vertical velocity is zero ($v_y = 0$). The instantaneous speed is purely horizontal: $v = u_x = u\cos\theta$.

progressive_hints.title: Perpendicular Acceleration
progressive_hints.text: Gravity acts strictly vertically downward, which is exactly perpendicular to the horizontal velocity vector at the apex. Thus $a_\perp = g$, giving $\rho = \frac{(u\cos\theta)^2}{g}$.

derivation_steps: The radius of curvature of any smooth planar trajectory is $\rho = \frac{v^2}{a_\perp}$, where $a_\perp$ is the component of acceleration perpendicular to instantaneous velocity $\vec{v}$.
At the apex of the projectile trajectory, the velocity vector is purely horizontal: $\vec{v}_{\text{apex}} = (u\cos\theta)\hat{i}$, so $v = u\cos\theta$.
The acceleration is $\vec{a} = -g\hat{j}$, which is perpendicular to $\hat{i}$.
Therefore, the normal acceleration is $a_\perp = g$.
Substituting: $\rho_{\text{apex}} = \frac{(u\cos\theta)^2}{g} = \frac{u^2\cos^2\theta}{g}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: rho -> u^2 / g (Recovers osculating circle of flat parabolic launch)
rho -> 0 (Path degenerates into a sharp needle turnaround of zero width)

questions.stem: The position of a particle moving along the x-axis is given by $x(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is in seconds (Figure KIN-05). During which of the following time intervals is the particle moving in the negative direction while speeding up?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Single particle with polynomial rectilinear position function

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Differentiating position to obtain velocity and acceleration, and finding the domain where v < 0 and a < 0 simultaneously.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires multi-derivative representation analysis and sign-matching for speeding up.

A.diagnostic: Correctly determined v(t) = 3(t-1)(t-3) < 0 for t in (1,3) and a(t) = 6(t-2) < 0 for t < 2, yielding overlap (1 s, 2 s).

B.diagnostic: Selected the interval where v > 0 and particle is moving forward while slowing down.

C.diagnostic: Selected (2 s, 3 s) where particle moves backward (v < 0) but slows down (a > 0).

D.diagnostic: Selected t > 3 s where particle moves in the positive direction and speeds up.

progressive_hints.title: Velocity and Acceleration Derivatives
progressive_hints.text: Compute $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 3(t-1)(t-3)$ and $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = 6t - 12 = 6(t-2)$.

progressive_hints.title: Condition for Moving in Negative Direction
progressive_hints.text: The particle moves in the negative direction when velocity is negative: $v(t) < 0 \implies 1 < t < 3\text{ s}$.

progressive_hints.title: Condition for Speeding Up
progressive_hints.text: An object speeds up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign. For negative velocity, we need $a(t) < 0 \implies t < 2\text{ s}$. The intersection is $1\text{ s} < t < 2\text{ s}$.

derivation_steps: Position: $x(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$.
Velocity: $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 3(t - 1)(t - 3)$.
Acceleration: $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = 6t - 12 = 6(t - 2)$.
Condition 1 (Moving in negative direction): $v(t) < 0 \iff (t - 1)(t - 3) < 0 \iff 1 < t < 3$.
Condition 2 (Speeding up): Speed is $|v(t)|$. $\frac{d}{dt}(v^2) = 2v a > 0 \implies v$ and $a$ have identical signs.
Since $v < 0$, we require $a < 0 \iff 6(t - 2) < 0 \iff t < 2$.
Taking the intersection of $1 < t < 3$ and $t < 2$ gives $1\text{ s} < t < 2\text{ s}$.

questions.stem: A river of width $W = 120\text{ m}$ flows at a constant speed of $v_r = 3\text{ m/s}$. A swimmer who can swim at $v_s = 5\text{ m/s}$ in still water wants to cross directly to the opposite bank with zero downstream drift. What is the time required for the swimmer to cross the river, and in what direction must they head?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Swimmer navigating flowing river channel
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial bank frame (+x downstream, +y perpendicular across)

options.A: Time $= 30\text{ s}$, heading at $\arcsin(3/5) \approx 36.9^\circ$ upstream of perpendicular
options.B: Time $= 24\text{ s}$, heading directly perpendicular to the bank

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Decomposing swimmer velocity to cancel river drift vs*sin(theta) = vr and computing perpendicular transit time W / (vs*cos(theta)).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires relative vector algebra and drift cancellation constraint.

A.diagnostic: Correctly determined sin(theta) = 3/5 => cos(theta) = 4/5, v_perp = 4 m/s, and t = 120 / 4 = 30 s.

B.diagnostic: Used t = W / v_s = 120 / 5 = 24 s, which produces significant downstream drift.

C.diagnostic: Guessed 45 degree angle and miscomputed resultant speed.

D.diagnostic: Added river and swimmer speed (5 + 3 = 8 m/s) incorrectly.

progressive_hints.title: Zero Drift Vector Condition
progressive_hints.text: For zero downstream drift, the resultant velocity vector in the ground frame must point purely perpendicular to the river banks: $\vec{v}_{\text{ground}} = v_\perp \hat{j}$.

progressive_hints.title: Upstream Angle Calculation

questions.stem: A particle is projected from level ground at an elevation angle of $\theta = 60^\circ$ with initial speed $u$. What is the ratio of the radius of curvature of the trajectory at the point of projection (launch) to that at the highest point (apex), $\frac{\rho_{\text{launch}}}{\rho_{\text{apex}}}$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Point projectile traversing parabolic arc

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating normal acceleration components at launch a_perp=g*cos(theta) and apex a_perp=g to deduce the ratio sec^3(theta) = 8.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires differential normal acceleration derivation at arbitrary trajectory points.

A.diagnostic: Correctly proved rho_launch / rho_apex = [u^2 / (g cos theta)] / [u^2 cos^2 theta / g] = 1 / cos^3 theta = sec^3(60) = 2^3 = 8.

B.diagnostic: Used 1 / cos^2(theta) = sec^2(60) = 4, forgetting the normal acceleration cosine factor at launch.

C.diagnostic: Used 1 / cos(theta) = sec(60) = 2.

D.diagnostic: Used sec^4(60) = 16.

progressive_hints.title: Formula for Radius of Curvature
progressive_hints.text: Radius of curvature is given by $\rho = \frac{v^2}{a_\perp}$, where $a_\perp$ is acceleration perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity.

progressive_hints.title: At Launch and Apex
progressive_hints.text: At launch: $v = u$, and $\vec{a}$ makes angle $\theta$ with the normal, so $a_\perp = g\cos\theta \implies \rho_{\text{launch}} = \frac{u^2}{g\cos\theta}$. At apex: $v = u\cos\theta, a_\perp = g \implies \rho_{\text{apex}} = \frac{u^2\cos^2\theta}{g}$.

progressive_hints.title: Ratio of Curvatures
progressive_hints.text: $\frac{\rho_{\text{launch}}}{\rho_{\text{apex}}} = \frac{u^2 / (g\cos\theta)}{u^2\cos^2\theta / g} = \frac{1}{\cos^3\theta} = \sec^3\theta$. For $\theta = 60^\circ$, $\cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2} \implies 2^3 = 8$.

derivation_steps: Radius of curvature definition: $\rho = \frac{v^2}{a_\perp}$.
At launch ($t = 0$): Velocity vector $\vec{u}$ is directed at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. Gravity $\vec{g}$ is vertical.
The component of $\vec{g}$ perpendicular to $\vec{u}$ is $a_{\perp, 0} = g\cos\theta$.
Hence: $\rho_{\text{launch}} = \frac{u^2}{g\cos\theta}$.
At apex: The velocity vector is purely horizontal, with magnitude $v = u\cos\theta$.
Gravity is vertical, so it is fully perpendicular to velocity: $a_{\perp, \text{apex}} = g$.
Hence: $\rho_{\text{apex}} = \frac{(u\cos\theta)^2}{g} = \frac{u^2\cos^2\theta}{g}$.
Taking the ratio: $\frac{\rho_{\text{launch}}}{\rho_{\text{apex}}} = \frac{u^2 / (g\cos\theta)}{u^2\cos^2\theta / g} = \frac{1}{\cos^3\theta} = \sec^3\theta$.
For $\theta = 60^\circ$, $\cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2} \implies \sec 60^\circ = 2$. Thus $\sec^3(60^\circ) = 2^3 = 8$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: sec^3(0) = 1 => rho_launch = rho_apex (Parabola apex is launch point)
sec^3(theta) -> infinity (Apex curvature collapses to zero radius)

questions.stem: A smooth inclined plane is tilted at an angle of $\beta = 30^\circ$ to the horizontal. A small elastic steel ball is released from rest vertically from a height $h = 5\text{ m}$ directly above the incline (Figure KIN-07). It collides elastically with the incline and bounces off into projectile motion. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the distance $L$ along the incline between the first impact point and the second impact point?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Bouncing elastic sphere on inclined surface
system_parameters.reference_frame: Tilted Cartesian frame with +x' down the incline, +y' normal to incline

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Setting up tilted coordinates x' along plane and y' normal, calculating rebound components and proving L = 8*h*sin(beta).

A.diagnostic: Correctly proved L = 8*h*sin(beta) = 8(5)(sin 30) = 40 * 0.5 = 20 m.

B.diagnostic: Used 4*h*sin(beta) = 10 m, forgetting the acceleration along the incline contribution.

C.diagnostic: Omitted the sin(beta) factor: 8h = 40 m.

progressive_hints.title: Impact Speed and Rebound Geometry
progressive_hints.text: Speed before first impact is $v_0 = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(10)(5)} = 10\text{ m/s}$ downward. Since the collision is elastic ($e=1$) and the normal is at $\beta = 30^\circ$ to the vertical, the rebound angle relative to the normal is $30^\circ$.

progressive_hints.title: Decompose into Incline Coordinates
progressive_hints.text: Along normal ($y'$): $u_{y'} = v_0\cos\beta, g_{y'} = g\cos\beta$. Along incline ($x'$): $u_{x'} = v_0\sin\beta, g_{x'} = g\sin\beta$.

progressive_hints.title: Flight Time and Range Along Incline
progressive_hints.text: Flight time is $T = \frac{2u_{y'}}{g_{y'}} = \frac{2v_0\cos\beta}{g\cos\beta} = \frac{2v_0}{g} = 2\text{ s}$. Distance along incline is $L = u_{x'}T + \frac{1}{2}g_{x'}T^2 = (10\sin 30)(2) + \frac{1}{2}(10\sin 30)(4) = 10 + 10 = 20\text{ m}$.

derivation_steps: Speed acquired during vertical fall of height $h$: $v_0 = \sqrt{2gh}$.
Choose coordinate axes: $x'$ directed down the plane, $y'$ directed normal to the plane.
Gravitational acceleration components: $g_{x'} = g\sin\beta$, $g_{y'} = g\cos\beta$.
Because impact is elastic ($e = 1$) on a frictionless plane, velocity along the plane is conserved: $u_{x'} = v_0\sin\beta$.
Velocity normal to the plane reverses magnitude: $u_{y'} = v_0\cos\beta$.
Time of flight between consecutive bounces (when $y' = 0$): $T = \frac{2u_{y'}}{g_{y'}} = \frac{2v_0\cos\beta}{g\cos\beta} = \frac{2v_0}{g}$.
Distance along the incline traversed during time $T$:
$L = u_{x'}T + \frac{1}{2}g_{x'}T^2 = (v_0\sin\beta)\left(\frac{2v_0}{g}\right) + \frac{1}{2}(g\sin\beta)\left(\frac{2v_0}{g}\right)^2$.
$L = \frac{2v_0^2\sin\beta}{g} + \frac{2v_0^2\sin\beta}{g} = \frac{4v_0^2\sin\beta}{g}$.
Substitute $v_0^2 = 2gh$: $L = \frac{4(2gh)\sin\beta}{g} = 8h\sin\beta$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A wide river of width $W = 120\text{ m}$ flows with a swift current of $v_r = 5\text{ m/s}$. A swimmer with maximum speed $v_s = 3\text{ m/s}$ in still water wishes to cross to the opposite bank. Since $v_r > v_s$, zero downstream drift is physically impossible. What is the minimum possible downstream drift $x_{\min}$ achievable by the swimmer upon reaching the opposite bank?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Swimmer navigating swift river current (vr > vs)

options.A: $x_{\min} = 160\text{ m}$, heading at angle $\arcsin(3/5) \approx 36.9^\circ$ upstream of perpendicular
options.B: $x_{\min} = 200\text{ m}$, heading directly perpendicular to the bank

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Constructing the tangent velocity hodograph from the origin to the circle of radius vs centered at (vr, 0) to find minimum drift angle and distance.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires extremum geometric optimization for non-holonomic velocity bounds.

A.diagnostic: Correctly proved sin(theta) = vs / vr = 3/5 and x_min = W * cot(theta) = 120 * (4/3) = 160 m.

B.diagnostic: Assumed heading perpendicular gives minimum drift: t = 120/3 = 40 s, drift = 5 * 40 = 200 m.

C.diagnostic: Guessed drift equals river width (120 m).

D.diagnostic: Headed downstream, maximizing drift rather than minimizing.

progressive_hints.title: Tangent Velocity Circle Hodograph
progressive_hints.text: The possible ground velocities $\vec{v} = \vec{v}_r + \vec{v}_s$ form a circle of radius $v_s = 3$ centered at $(v_r, 0) = (5, 0)$. Drift is minimized when the line from the origin is tangent to this circle.

progressive_hints.title: Tangent Triangle Angle
progressive_hints.text: At tangency, the radius vector $\vec{v}_s$ is perpendicular to the resultant ground velocity $\vec{v}$. Therefore, $\sin\theta = \frac{v_s}{v_r} = \frac{3}{5}$, where $\theta$ is the angle with the perpendicular.

progressive_hints.title: Minimum Drift Distance
progressive_hints.text: The angle of resultant ground motion satisfies $\tan\phi = \frac{v_y}{v_x} = \frac{\sqrt{v_r^2 - v_s^2}}{v_s} = \frac{4}{3}$. Downstream drift is $x_{\min} = W \cot\phi = 120 \times \frac{4}{3} = 160\text{ m}$.

derivation_steps: Let $\theta$ be the angle of swimmer's heading upstream of the perpendicular bank normal.
Swimmer's velocity in ground frame: $v_x = v_r - v_s\sin\theta$, $v_y = v_s\cos\theta$.
Transit time to cross width $W$: $t = \frac{W}{v_y} = \frac{W}{v_s\cos\theta}$.
Downstream drift: $x(\theta) = v_x t = (v_r - v_s\sin\theta)\frac{W}{v_s\cos\theta} = W\left(\frac{v_r}{v_s}\sec\theta - \tan\theta\right)$.
To minimize $x(\theta)$, differentiate with respect to $\theta$ and set to zero:
$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = W\left(\frac{v_r}{v_s}\sec\theta\tan\theta - \sec^2\theta\right) = 0$.
$\implies \frac{v_r}{v_s}\tan\theta = \sec\theta \implies \frac{v_r}{v_s}\sin\theta = 1 \implies \sin\theta = \frac{v_s}{v_r}$.
Substitute $v_s = 3\text{ m/s}, v_r = 5\text{ m/s}$: $\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5} \implies \cos\theta = \frac{4}{5}, \tan\theta = \frac{3}{4}$.
Minimum drift: $x_{\min} = W\left(\frac{5}{3}\left(\frac{5}{4}\right) - \frac{3}{4}\right) = W\left(\frac{25}{12} - \frac{9}{12}\right) = W\left(\frac{16}{12}\right) = W\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)$.
For $W = 120\text{ m}$: $x_{\min} = 120 \times \frac{4}{3} = 160\text{ m}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: sqrt(v_r^2 - v_s^2) -> 0 => x_min -> 0 (Zero drift becomes marginally achievable at theta = 90 deg)
x_min -> infinity (Never reaches opposite bank)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Two particles are projected simultaneously from the same point on level ground with equal speed $u = 20\text{ m/s}$ in opposite directions: Particle 1 to the right at an elevation angle of $\alpha = 60^\circ$, and Particle 2 to the left at an elevation angle of $\beta = 30^\circ$. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, at what time $t$ after launch do their velocity vectors $\vec{v}_1(t)$ and $\vec{v}_2(t)$ become mutually perpendicular?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two projectiles launched simultaneously in opposing directions
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame (+x to the right, +y upward)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Expressing time-dependent velocity vectors v1(t) and v2(t), setting vector dot product v1 . v2 = 0, and discovering exact algebraic cancellation.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires vector orthogonality modeling and kinematic dot-product algebraic reduction.

A.diagnostic: Correctly proved v1 . v2 = 0 yields t = u*(sin 60 + sin 30) / g = 20 * ((sqrt(3) + 1)/2) / 10 = sqrt(3) + 1 approx 2.73 s.

B.diagnostic: Estimated sqrt(3) + 1 as approx 2 s.

C.diagnostic: Subtracted angles or inverted the root sign to sqrt(3) - 1 s.

D.diagnostic: Averaged total flight times.

progressive_hints.title: Vector Velocity Expressions
progressive_hints.text: Particle 1: $\vec{v}_1(t) = u\cos 60^\circ\hat{i} + (u\sin 60^\circ - gt)\hat{j}$. Particle 2 (opposite direction): $\vec{v}_2(t) = -u\cos 30^\circ\hat{i} + (u\sin 30^\circ - gt)\hat{j}$.

progressive_hints.title: Perpendicularity Condition
progressive_hints.text: Two vectors are perpendicular if and only if their scalar dot product is zero: $\vec{v}_1(t) \cdot \vec{v}_2(t) = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Dot Product and Cancellation
progressive_hints.text: Notice that $-u^2\cos 60^\circ\cos 30^\circ + u^2\sin 60^\circ\sin 30^\circ = -u^2(\frac{1}{2})(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) + u^2(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})(\frac{1}{2}) = 0$! This leaves $-gt u(\sin 60^\circ + \sin 30^\circ) + g^2 t^2 = 0 \implies t = \frac{u(\sin 60^\circ + \sin 30^\circ)}{g} = \sqrt{3} + 1\text{ s}$.

derivation_steps: Velocity of Particle 1: $\vec{v}_1(t) = u\cos\alpha\hat{i} + (u\sin\alpha - gt)\hat{j}$.
Velocity of Particle 2 (launched in negative x direction): $\vec{v}_2(t) = -u\cos\beta\hat{i} + (u\sin\beta - gt)\hat{j}$.
Perpendicular condition: $\vec{v}_1(t) \cdot \vec{v}_2(t) = 0$.
Expanding the dot product:
$-u^2\cos\alpha\cos\beta + (u\sin\alpha - gt)(u\sin\beta - gt) = 0$.
$-u^2\cos\alpha\cos\beta + u^2\sin\alpha\sin\beta - gt u(\sin\alpha + \sin\beta) + g^2 t^2 = 0$.
For $\alpha = 60^\circ$ and $\beta = 30^\circ$:
$\cos 60^\circ\cos 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$, and $\sin 60^\circ\sin 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$.
The initial constant terms cancel identically: $-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}u^2 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}u^2 = 0$!
The equation reduces to: $g^2 t^2 - gt u(\sin 60^\circ + \sin 30^\circ) = 0$.
For $t > 0$, dividing by $gt$: $gt = u(\sin 60^\circ + \sin 30^\circ)$.
$t = \frac{u}{g}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{20}{10}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{2}\right) = \sqrt{3} + 1\text{ s} \approx 2.732\text{ s}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: t -> 0 (Stationary particles)

limiting_cases.condition: Dot product verification at t = sqrt(3)+1
limiting_cases.expected_outcome: v1 = 10 i - 10 j; v2 = -10*sqrt(3) i - 10*sqrt(3) j; v1 . v2 = -100*sqrt(3) + 100*sqrt(3) = 0 (Strictly perpendicular confirmed)
